compression.title: Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts
compression.lede: is a Plano, Texas non-profit, founded by Daniel B. Wallace in 2002, that photographs Greek New Testament manuscripts held by others and publishes the images, so the text read today reflects what was first written, and as "scientific evidence (against the claims of skeptics)" (csntm.org; Wikipedia; RF record).

sentences.text: The Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts (CSNTM) is, in the Revelation First record's kind, "a center that digitizes Greek New Testament manuscripts and publishes their images in a searchable digital manuscript collection" (RF record), a 501(c)(3) non-profit whose mission is "to digitally preserve Greek New Testament manuscripts", photographing them at "institutions, libraries, museums, monasteries, universities, and archives around the world" (Wikipedia; its LinkedIn page), under the motto "Preserving the Ancient Text for Generation Next" (csntm.org).

Its own pages set the preservation inside a purpose: "ensuring that the New Testament you read most accurately reflects the original words of the apostles and early witnesses of Jesus Christ" (csntm.org, 25 August 2026), "preserving the accuracy of the New Testament text and tracing its history through the ages" (its North Texas Giving Day profile), so that readers "hold in their hands the most accurate text possible" (csntm.org).

The Scribal Fellowship, its monthly-giving community "Modeled after the support once given to ancient scribes", is offered three objectives: that "modern publications of the New Testament accurately reflect the words first written in the first century", that the manuscripts be preserved "against decay, loss, and destruction", and "scientific evidence (against the claims of skeptics) that what we have today is, indeed, what they wrote then" (csntm.org); the Revelation First record reads the third as making the center "NOT a neutral archive" (RF record).

Daniel B. Wallace founded it in 2002 "to digitize all surviving Greek manuscripts of the New Testament" (csntm.org), in September 2002 by Wikipedia and the center's profile, "to photograph and fully archive all known Greek New Testament manuscripts"; he is its "founder and Executive Director", and it is at 2001 W. Plano Parkway, Plano, Texas (csntm.org; Wikipedia; the Facebook card; RF record).

Wikipedia's infobox adds a Chairman of the Board, Michael W. Holmes, and a parent organization, the "Center for the Research of Early Christian Documents", which the record's operator field does not name (Wikipedia; RF record).

The method answers the microfilms: "The microfilm images are helpful, but many times they are unclear. For this reason, CSNTM has been producing high-resolution photographs of these documents" (csntm.org); the record gives it as "high-resolution digital photography of manuscripts held by other institutions, catalogued and published online" (RF record), and the Capture Registry finds that lineage, "the microfilms it answers", absent from the composition at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The archive defines what such an image is: the photograph of a handwritten page is "a *new* object made at a particular moment under particular light, and no two photographs of one page share a digest", so that an identifier computed over a capture "identifies **that capture**, not the artifact" (#1443).

The collection mixes kinds of image: its search offers "Digital Facsimile", "Digital Microfilm" and "Digital MSI" beside its own photographs, and some entries carry images "made available by the British Library" or by the holding institution (manuscripts.csntm.org); the digitization literature #1443 surveys finds the surrogate "layered and lossy in ways the result conceals", a photograph of a microfilm its standing exemplum (#1443, reporting that literature).

Of that literature #1443 adds that it "has no account of the object entering machine reading, and it works — like the whole papyrological stack — on collections whose creators cannot be asked" (#1443).

Since 2018 the center has used multispectral imaging, made portable (Wikipedia), most recently in Oslo "to examine the authenticity of 31 fragments" of the Schøyen Dead Sea Scroll collection (csntm.org, 24 September 2026).

Its counts differ by source and date: "hundreds of institutions in more than 50 countries" since 2002 (csntm.org); "more than 45 institutions on 4 continents" and "nearly 300,000 images from approximately 700 New Testament manuscripts" (Wikipedia, as of 2019, marked as needing a citation; the center's profile, as of 2022).

So do its discoveries: "as many as 17" manuscripts at the National Library of Greece not catalogued by the INTF, the oldest seventh-century, and "more than 90 New Testament manuscripts" since 2002 (Associates for Biblical Research, 28 January 2016); 21 unknown to the INTF digitized at that library (Wikipedia); "over 75" (Wikipedia, 2019; the profile, 2022, "more than any other organization in the 21st century"); and "almost 60 previously unknown manuscripts that can now be found in the official catalog" (csntm.org).

The Capture Registry reads the composition's "nearly 90" against the home page's "almost 60" as the discoveries enlarged, its PER reader allowing that the gap "may be a later count the record does not carry" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); the earlier count, "more than 90" since 2002, is the Associates for Biblical Research's of 2016 (ABR).

The official catalogue those discoveries enter is the INTF's, which "maintains the official catalog of New Testament Greek manuscripts, and edits and publishes the standard critical editions" (csntm.org, its history of the discipline); the record keeps the center apart from that work: "NOT an edition: it publishes images and catalogue descriptions" (RF record).

The record's worked question gives the difference, "An image lets a reader check a reading; an edition reports one", and names the center for "images of Greek New Testament manuscripts, searchable by type and century" (RF record); the archive sets textual criticism, which "spent twenty-three centuries developing technologies for making interpretive supply visible, contestable, and revisable", against the composition layer's "apparatus of *unmarked* supply" (#1422).

The images are online in the Digital Manuscript Collection, where "Scholars visit the website to study manuscript images as they edit the text that stands behind English translations" (csntm.org); Wikipedia calls them "freely accessible", with more than 50,000 users a year (unsourced), and the profile "freely accessed", its images "the foundation for the modern translations of the New Testament" (Wikipedia; North Texas Giving Day).

The search page binds their use: "Your continued use of CSNTM.org demonstrates your willingness to agree to our Terms of Use and Copyright policy", any use of the images to go through the center (manuscripts.csntm.org); the record gives access "on agreement to its Terms of Use and Copyright policy", the terms "not read" (RF record), and the Capture Registry finds the composition's "freely available" carrying none of them: "the terms are not carried" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The record holds that it is "NOT the holding institution: it photographs manuscripts held by others" (RF record); Wikipedia records that in October 2005 the center "acquired a tenth or eleventh century minuscule of the Gospel of Luke on parchment", later catalogued as Gregory–Aland 2882 (Wikipedia).

Its unit is the manuscript, classed "Papyrus Majuscule Minuscule Lectionary" and dated by century, with images and a short description (manuscripts.csntm.org; RF record), the kinds of evidence images and catalogue, from holding institutions worldwide and from the second century on as the century filter runs; the search as saved returned "2045 results", the profile counts "more than 2,000" and Wikipedia, in 2019, "more than 1,700", and Septuagint papyri stand beside the New Testament (manuscripts.csntm.org; North Texas Giving Day; Wikipedia; RF record).

Among its collections are the Chester Beatty papyri, digitized in 2013: P46, "the oldest manuscript of Paul's letters—dated c. AD 200", P45, and P47, "the oldest manuscript of Revelation—3rd century" (Wikipedia); the center "photographed the images of the three manuscripts and produced this facsimile in partnership with the holding institutions and the publisher, Hendrickson", P47 "one of the oldest manuscripts of Revelation with only ten leaves", and reads P45 and P46 as showing New Testament writings "compiled into one book" by the third century in some places (csntm.org; RF record).

Its blog carries Daniel B. Wallace on the photographs that made "three of the earliest and most extensive New Testament papyri" available nearly nine decades ago, and Peter Malik's guest post "The Chester Beatty Papyrus of Revelation (P47): New Finds from an Old Treasure Trove" (csntm.org; RF record).

Its catalogue dates the earliest papyri by century: P52, the Gospels, "Second century"; P98, Revelation, "Possible second century"; P46, Paul, "c. 200"; P47, Revelation, "Late third century" (manuscripts.csntm.org); the archive's work plan gives 𝔓46, the "Chester Beatty II codex", as c. 175–225 CE, "The earliest physical witness to any Pauline letter" (#832).

On those copies the archive states its papyrological inversion: "The material record disturbs the received confidence hierarchy", the earliest witness Johannine (𝔓52), not Pauline (𝔓46), the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (#202), and, earlier, Revelation "among the earliest NT texts preserved in manuscript fragments (P18, P47, P98)", so that "The textual record does not contradict first-composition" (#636).

Its rule and its limits are stated with it: "Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties", and where composition dates are inferential "material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority" (#202); "The section does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates", only that the machinery dating Paul ahead of the material evidence is as speculative as an early date for Revelation, the discipline's refusal of the asymmetry "evidence of consensus-maintenance" (#832); and the thesis is falsified if "a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation" (#202).

The Revelation First record reads the center there: "P47, the Chester Beatty papyrus of Revelation, and the Pauline P46 are among its imaged papyri", and "the images are where those copies can be read" (RF record, the archive's reading), under the census's correction, "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early" (RF record).

The record asks of each resource "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", places the center at papyrology and textual discovery and at New Testament scholarship, and answers that it shows "where images of P47 (Revelation) and P46 (Paul) can be examined" and not "when Revelation was composed: a manuscript's century dates the copy" (RF record).

Its worked question on the papyri names the center for those images "with century dates as catalogued" and records that no record gives "a sourced date and dating method for P47" (RF record); the catalogue gives P47 as "Late third century" and states no method (manuscripts.csntm.org).

The record finds no stated limits in its saved sources, leaves the manuscript records, the full P47 post and the Terms of Use unchecked, names Oxyrhynchus Online a neighbour without cross-reference, and keeps the center active, "digitizing, training interns and publishing" (RF record), its internship having "helped develop 30% of the rising New Testament textual scholars over the past ten years" (North Texas Giving Day); Wikipedia's article on it is marked "This article needs more citations." (Wikipedia, August 2025).

At its name the composition layer gives who founded it, where it is, what it does and how its images are reached "from the center's own site and five pages about it", founder, year, place and mission all the record's, the center and Wallace named with no identifier, no inversion and no standing substitution, at a new address whose cards do not cite the record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry reads it as "composed by its method alone", keeping "the camera" and dropping "the argument the camera serves": the apologetic aim "is the center's own sentence, and the composition leaves it out", so "the census's 'NOT a neutral archive' does not survive"; and "The composition names no manuscript" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

O202-01.quote: The material record disturbs the received confidence hierarchy. The earliest physical NT witness is Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE), not Pauline (𝔓46, usually dated c. 175–225 CE). The earliest physical copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98, usually dated c. 150–175 CE) predates the earliest physical copy of Romans.
O202-01.source_label: #202 Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early The Apocalypse as the Earliest New Testament Document

O636-01.quote: **Papyrological record.** Revelation is among the earliest NT texts preserved in manuscript fragments (P18, P47, P98), contemporaneous with or preceding fragments of John and Paul. The textual record does not contradict first-composition.
